pairs.right: Return if bought today and held to maturity
Coupon rate < market rate, price < par
Coupon rate > market rate, price > par
Issuer can retire it before maturity
Pays for the chance the issuer won't pay
Extra yield for longer, more rate-sensitive bonds
Extra yield for bonds that are hard to sell
Coupons may have to be reinvested at lower rates

hints.title: Equal-risk bonds
lines: Equal risk → same EAR, not the same nominal rate
Semiannual → annual: EAR = (1 + YTM/2)^{2} − 1
Annual → semiannual: i = (1 + EAR)^{1/2} − 1

hints.title: Raising money with bonds
lines: Price one bond with the required return
Bonds needed = amount to raise ÷ price per bond (round up)

hints.title: Pricing a bond
lines: Semiannual: N = years × 2, i = YTM / 2, PMT = coupon / 2
Quarterly: N = years × 4, i = YTM / 4, PMT = coupon / 4
Zero-coupon: P = FV / (1 + i)^{N}
Calculator: N, I/Y, PMT, FV → CPT PV

hints.title: Yields
lines: YTM: enter PV as negative, CPT I/Y (× 2 if semiannual)
Current yield = annual coupon ÷ price
Coupon rate = annual coupon ÷ face value

hints.title: Bond features & risks
lines: Bond = loan to the issuer (debt), not ownership
YTM = risk-free + default + liquidity + maturity premiums
Better rating → lower yield → higher price
Longer maturity → more sensitive to rate changes
Higher expected inflation → higher yields → lower prices

hints.title: Bond rules of thumb
lines: Rates up → prices down (inverse relationship)
Coupon > YTM → premium; coupon < YTM → discount; equal → par
Price pulls toward par as maturity approaches

questions.question: When you buy a bond, you are:
choices: Becoming an owner of the issuer
Buying an option on its stock
questions.explanation: A bond is a debt instrument: the bondholder lends to the issuer, who pays periodic interest and repays principal at maturity.

questions.question: A $1,000 bond pays $60 of interest per year. Its coupon rate is:
choices: It depends on the market price
questions.explanation: Coupon rate = annual coupon ÷ face value = 60 / 1,000 = 6%. It doesn't depend on the market price.

questions.question: Bonds issued by the World Bank, the EIB or the IMF are called:
A HIGHER credit rating generally means:
choices: Higher default risk and a higher yield
Lower default risk and a higher price
A bond that can no longer be traded
A bond that stops paying coupons
A bond that is always callable early
questions.explanation: Ratings (Moody's, S&P, Fitch) assess creditworthiness. Better rating → lower default risk → lower required yield → higher price.

questions.question: Compared with developed-market bonds, emerging-market bonds typically:
choices: Have lower yields because those economies grow faster
Are seen as riskier, so they offer higher yields
Carry no default risk because governments back them
Must always be issued in U.S. dollars
Can only be bought by local investors

questions.question: Which is NOT one of the components of a bond's YTM?
questions.explanation: YTM = risk-free rate + default risk premium + liquidity premium + maturity premium.

questions.question: Newly issued 'on-the-run' bonds are:
choices: Less liquid, so they need a higher yield
More liquid, so they need a lower yield
Not traded until they are a year old

questions.question: Market interest rates rise by 1%. Which bond's price falls the MOST?
questions.explanation: Longer maturity → greater sensitivity to interest-rate changes (that's why there's a maturity premium).

questions.question: A public offering of bonds is usually done with the help of:
questions.explanation: The investment bank determines funding needs, structures the debt, drafts the indenture, registers the issue, prices it and sells it.

questions.question: Because the price–yield curve is convex, a 1% DROP in rates causes:
choices: A smaller price change than a 1% rise
A bigger price gain than the loss from a 1% rise
No price change because coupons are fixed
Exactly the same size of price change as a 1% rise in rates
The bond to be called by the issuer

questions.question: Bond A matures in 5 years, has a $1,000 face value and a 10% annual coupon. If the market rate is 10%, its price is:
questions.explanation: Coupon rate = market rate → the bond sells at par.

questions.question: Bond A (5 years, $1,000 face, 10% annual coupon). If the market rate rises to 12%, the price becomes:
questions.explanation: N = 5, I/Y = 12, PMT = 100, FV = 1,000 → PV = $927.90. Coupon < market → discount.

questions.question: Bond A (5 years, $1,000 face, 10% annual coupon). If the market rate falls to 8%, the price becomes:
questions.explanation: N = 5, I/Y = 8, PMT = 100, FV = 1,000 → PV = $1,079.85. Coupon > market → premium.

questions.question: An IBM bond pays $115 every year for 5 years, plus $1,000 at the end. The bond is rated AAA and AAA bonds yield 7.5%. What is it worth?
What is the price of a 7.25% annual coupon bond with a $1,000 face value that matures in 3 years, if the required return is 0.35%?
A 3-year government bond has a 4.25% annual coupon rate, paid semiannually ($1,000 face). Investors demand a nominal 0.965% return, compounded semiannually. What is the price?
A bond pays $50 every six months for 10 years ($1,000 face). The YTM is 8% compounded semiannually. What is its price?
A bond pays a $25 semiannual coupon, matures in 3 years and 1 month, and has a 6% nominal YTM compounded semiannually. What is its price?
With a discount rate of 3% per period, what is a 5-period zero-coupon bond with a $1,000 par value worth?
questions.explanation: P = 1,000 / 1.03^5 = $862.61. Zeros always sell at a discount.

questions.question: A $1,000 par bond has a 7% annual coupon, 9 years to maturity and a required return of 10%. Its price is $827.23. What is its current yield?
A bond's quoted YTM is 6% compounded semiannually. What is the equivalent effective annual rate (EAR)?
A bond's price is quoted as 112.905 (percent of par). With a $1,000 par value, how much does it cost?
questions.explanation: 112.905% × $1,000 = $1,129.05. (The slide prints $1,120.05, which is a typo.)

questions.question: Bonds represent ownership in a company similar to stocks.
questions.explanation: Bonds are debt (a loan to the issuer), not ownership.

questions.question: A bond selling at a discount must have a higher coupon than market rate.
questions.explanation: A discount bond has a coupon rate LOWER than the market rate.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a feature of a bond?
questions.explanation: A bond's price changes with market rates, so there's no fixed selling price.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is most correct regarding the nominal risk-free rate?
choices: It is equal to the real rate of return minus expected inflation.
It reflects only the growth of the economy.
It includes both the real rate of return and an adjustment for expected inflation.
It is unaffected by changes in inflation expectations.
questions.explanation: Nominal risk-free rate = real rate of return + expected inflation.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is most correct regarding the components of Yield to Maturity (YTM)?
choices: The risk-free rate compensates investors for the possibility that the issuer may default.
The liquidity premium is higher for bonds that are easier to sell quickly.
The maturity premium reflects the increased sensitivity of long-term bonds to interest rate changes.
The default risk premium is only relevant for government bonds.

questions.question: A 12-year bond has an annual coupon rate of 9%. The coupon rate will remain fixed until the bond matures. The bond currently has a yield to maturity (YTM) of 7%. Which of the following statements is most correct?
choices: The bond is currently selling at a price below its par value.
If market interest rates decline today, the price of the bond will also decline today.
If market interest rates remain unchanged, the bond's price one year from now will be lower than it is today.
All of the statements above are correct.
None of the statements above is correct.
questions.explanation: Coupon 9% > YTM 7%, so it's a premium bond (a is false). Rates down → price up (b is false). With an unchanged YTM, a premium bond's price falls toward par over time (c is true).

questions.question: A 10-year corporate bond has an annual coupon payment of 9 percent. The bond is currently selling at par ($1,000). Which of the following statements is most correct?
choices: The bond's yield to maturity is 9 percent.
The bond's current yield is 9 percent.
If the bond's yield to maturity remains constant, the bond's price will remain at par.
Statements a and c are correct.
All of the statements above are correct.
questions.explanation: At par: YTM = coupon rate = 9%, current yield = 90/1,000 = 9%, and with a constant YTM the price stays at par.

questions.question: If inflation expectations rise, bond prices:
questions.explanation: Higher expected inflation raises nominal required yields, and higher yields mean lower prices.

questions.question: A 12-year bond has a 9 percent annual coupon, a yield to maturity of 8 percent, and a face value of $1,000. What is the price of the bond?
A corporate bond has a face value of $1,000, and pays 10 percent semiannual coupon. The bond matures in 12 years and sells at a price of $1,080. What is the bond's nominal yield to maturity?
questions.explanation: N = 24, PV = −1,080, PMT = 50, FV = 1,000 → I/Y = 4.45% per half-year → nominal YTM = 8.90%.

questions.question: A bond that matures in 12 years has a 9 percent semiannual coupon and a face value of $1,000. The bond has a nominal yield to maturity of 8 percent. What is the price of the bond today?

Your client has been offered a 5-year, $1,000 par value bond with a 10 percent coupon. Interest on this bond is paid quarterly. If your client is to earn a nominal rate of return of 12 percent, compounded quarterly, how much should she pay for the bond?

A 20-year bond with a par value of $1,000 has a 9 percent annual coupon. The bond currently sells for $925. If the bond's yield to maturity remains at its current rate, what will be the price of the bond 5 years from now?

You just purchased a 15-year bond with an 11 percent annual coupon. The bond has a face value of $1,000 and a current yield of 10 percent. Assuming that the yield to maturity of 9.7072 percent remains constant, what will be the price of the bond one year from now?

Cold Boxes Ltd. has 100 bonds outstanding (maturity value = $1,000). The nominal required rate of return on these bonds is currently 10 percent, and interest is paid semiannually. The bonds mature in 5 years, and their current market value is $768 per bond. What is the annual coupon interest rate?
questions.explanation: N = 10, I/Y = 5, PV = −768, FV = 1,000 → PMT = $19.95 per half-year ≈ $40 per year → coupon rate ≈ 4%.

questions.question: The current price of a 10-year, $1,000 par value bond is $1,158.91. Interest on this bond is paid every six months, and the nominal annual yield is 14 percent. Given these facts, what is the annual coupon rate on this bond?
A 16-year bond with a 10 percent annual coupon has a current yield of 8 percent. What is the bond's yield to maturity (YTM)?

A 7-year bond that pays 9 percent interest semiannually sells for $1,040. Another 7-year bond of equal risk pays 9 percent interest annually. Both bonds are noncallable and have face values of $1,000. What is the price of the bond that pays annual interest?
questions.explanation: Semiannual bond: N = 14, PV = −1,040, PMT = 45 → 4.118% per half → EAR = 1.04118² − 1 = 8.406%. Equal risk → same EAR. Annual bond: N = 7, I/Y = 8.406, PMT = 90, FV = 1,000 → $1,030.48.

questions.question: Assume that you are considering the purchase of a $1,000 par value bond that pays interest of $70 each six months and has 10 years to go before it matures. If you buy this bond, you expect to hold it for 5 years and then to sell it in the market. You (and other investors) currently require a nominal annual rate of 16 percent, but you expect the market to require a nominal rate of only 12 percent when you sell the bond due to a general decline in interest rates. How much should you be willing to pay for this bond?

An 8 percent annual coupon, noncallable bond has 10 years until it matures and a yield to maturity of 9.1 percent. What should be the price of a 10-year noncallable bond of equal risk that pays an 8 percent semiannual coupon? Assume both bonds have a par value of $1,000.
A 10-year, $1,000 par value bond pays interest annually. It sells for $903.73 and has a yield to maturity of 9%. What is its coupon rate?
A 10-year, $1,000 par bond has a 12% coupon rate paid semiannually. Its nominal yield to maturity is 10%. What is the bond's price?
A 20-year, $1,000 par bond pays an 8% coupon semiannually. The nominal yield to maturity is 10%. What is the bond worth today?
A 10-year bond has an 8% annual coupon rate paid semiannually and a $1,000 face value. If the nominal yield to maturity is 9%, what is its price?
A 10-year, $1,000 par bond pays $50 every six months. The nominal yield to maturity is 9%. What is the bond's price?
A 15-year, $1,000 par bond has an 8% coupon paid semiannually. Investors require a nominal return of 11%. What should the bond sell for?
A 12-year, $1,000 par bond pays an 8% coupon semiannually and has a nominal yield to maturity of 7%. What is its price?
A 10-year, $1,000 par bond has a 14% coupon rate paid quarterly. If the nominal yield to maturity is 12%, compounded quarterly, what is the bond's price?
An 11-year, $1,000 par bond pays an 8% annual coupon and currently sells for $865. What is its yield to maturity?
questions.explanation: N = 11, PV = −865, PMT = 80, FV = 1,000 → I/Y = 10.09%. (80 / 865 = 9.25% is only the current yield.)

questions.question: A bond of equal risk pays interest semiannually and has a nominal yield to maturity of 8%. What is the price of a 6-year, $1,000 par bond that pays an 8% coupon ANNUALLY?
questions.explanation: Equal risk → same EAR. EAR = (1 + 0.08/2)² − 1 = 8.16%. Then N = 6, I/Y = 8.16, PMT = 80, FV = 1,000 → PV = $992.64. (Using 8% directly would wrongly give $1,000.)

questions.question: Equal-risk bonds pay semiannually with a nominal yield to maturity of 9%. What is the price of a 10-year, $1,000 par bond that pays a 9% coupon once a year?
A 15-year, $1,000 par bond pays an 8% coupon semiannually. Market rates have jumped and investors now require a nominal 16% return. What is the bond worth?
questions.explanation: N = 15 × 2 = 30, I/Y = 16 / 2 = 8, PMT = 80 / 2 = 40, FV = 1,000 → PV = $549.69. A deep discount: the coupon is half the required return.

questions.question: A company needs to raise $2,000,000 by selling 10-year, $1,000 par bonds with an 8% coupon paid semiannually ($40 every six months). Equal-risk bonds pay $60 every six months and sell at par, so investors require 6% per half-year. How many bonds must it sell?
questions.explanation: Required return = 60 / 1,000 = 6% per period. N = 20, I/Y = 6, PMT = 40, FV = 1,000 → PV = $770.60. Bonds = 2,000,000 / 770.60 = 2,595.4, so round up to 2,596.

questions.question: Equal-risk bonds pay semiannually and have a nominal yield to maturity of 7%. What is the price of a 12-year, $1,000 par bond with a 7% annual coupon paid once a year?
A 15-year, $1,000 par bond has a 15% coupon rate paid quarterly. The nominal yield to maturity is 12%, compounded quarterly. What is the bond's price?
